text: Prove that $\frac{\tan\theta+\sec\theta-1}{\tan\theta-\sec\theta+1}=\frac{1+\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}$.
answer: LHS $=\frac{(\tan\theta+\sec\theta)-(\sec^{2}\theta-\tan^{2}\theta)}{\tan\theta-\sec\theta+1}$, using $1=\sec^{2}\theta-\tan^{2}\theta$ in the numerator. Since $\sec^{2}\theta-\tan^{2}\theta=(\sec\theta+\tan\theta)(\sec\theta-\tan\theta)$, the numerator is $(\sec\theta+\tan\theta)\left[1-(\sec\theta-\tan\theta)\right]=(\sec\theta+\tan\theta)(1-\sec\theta+\tan\theta)$. The bracket equals the denominator $\tan\theta-\sec\theta+1$, so LHS $=\sec\theta+\tan\theta=\frac{1}{\cos\theta}+\frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}=\frac{1+\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}=$ RHS.

text: Prove that $\frac{\cot A+\operatorname{cosec}A-1}{\cot A-\operatorname{cosec}A+1}=\frac{1+\cos A}{\sin A}$.
answer: Using $1=\operatorname{cosec}^{2}A-\cot^{2}A$, numerator $=(\operatorname{cosec}A+\cot A)-(\operatorname{cosec}A+\cot A)(\operatorname{cosec}A-\cot A)$ $=(\operatorname{cosec}A+\cot A)(1-\operatorname{cosec}A+\cot A)$. The second factor is the denominator $\cot A-\operatorname{cosec}A+1$, so LHS $=\operatorname{cosec}A+\cot A=\frac{1}{\sin A}+\frac{\cos A}{\sin A}=\frac{1+\cos A}{\sin A}=$ RHS.

text: Prove that $\frac{\sin\theta-\cos\theta+1}{\sin\theta+\cos\theta-1}+\frac{\sin\theta+\cos\theta-1}{\sin\theta-\cos\theta+1}=2\sec\theta$.
answer: Divide numerator and denominator of the first fraction by $\cos\theta$: $\frac{\tan\theta-1+\sec\theta}{\tan\theta+1-\sec\theta}$. Write the $1$ in the numerator as $\sec^{2}\theta-\tan^{2}\theta$: numerator $=(\tan\theta+\sec\theta)-(\sec\theta+\tan\theta)(\sec\theta-\tan\theta)=(\sec\theta+\tan\theta)(1-\sec\theta+\tan\theta)$. The second factor is the denominator, so the first fraction $=\sec\theta+\tan\theta$. The second fraction is its reciprocal: $\frac{1}{\sec\theta+\tan\theta}=\frac{\sec\theta-\tan\theta}{\sec^{2}\theta-\tan^{2}\theta}=\sec\theta-\tan\theta$. Hence LHS $=(\sec\theta+\tan\theta)+(\sec\theta-\tan\theta)=2\sec\theta=$ RHS.

text: Prove that $(1+\cot\theta-\operatorname{cosec}\theta)(1+\tan\theta+\sec\theta)=2$.
answer: LHS $=\left(1+\frac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}-\frac{1}{\sin\theta}\right)\left(1+\frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}+\frac{1}{\cos\theta}\right)=\frac{(\sin\theta+\cos\theta-1)(\sin\theta+\cos\theta+1)}{\sin\theta\cos\theta}$. Numerator $=(\sin\theta+\cos\theta)^{2}-1=\sin^{2}\theta+\cos^{2}\theta+2\sin\theta\cos\theta-1=2\sin\theta\cos\theta$. So LHS $=\frac{2\sin\theta\cos\theta}{\sin\theta\cos\theta}=2=$ RHS.

text: Prove that $\frac{\tan\theta}{\sec\theta-1}+\frac{\tan\theta}{\sec\theta+1}=2\operatorname{cosec}\theta$.
answer: LHS $=\tan\theta\cdot\frac{(\sec\theta+1)+(\sec\theta-1)}{\sec^{2}\theta-1}=\frac{2\tan\theta\sec\theta}{\tan^{2}\theta}=\frac{2\sec\theta}{\tan\theta}$. Now $\frac{\sec\theta}{\tan\theta}=\frac{1}{\cos\theta}\cdot\frac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}=\frac{1}{\sin\theta}$, so LHS $=2\operatorname{cosec}\theta=$ RHS.

text: Prove that $\frac{\cos\theta-\cos^{3}\theta}{\sin\theta-\sin^{3}\theta}=\tan\theta$.
answer: Numerator $=\cos\theta(1-\cos^{2}\theta)=\cos\theta\sin^{2}\theta$. Denominator $=\sin\theta(1-\sin^{2}\theta)=\sin\theta\cos^{2}\theta$. So LHS $=\frac{\cos\theta\sin^{2}\theta}{\sin\theta\cos^{2}\theta}=\frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}=\tan\theta=$ RHS.

text: If $x=a\sec\theta+b\tan\theta$ and $y=a\tan\theta+b\sec\theta$, prove that $x^{2}-y^{2}=a^{2}-b^{2}$.
answer: $x^{2}=a^{2}\sec^{2}\theta+2ab\sec\theta\tan\theta+b^{2}\tan^{2}\theta$ and $y^{2}=a^{2}\tan^{2}\theta+2ab\sec\theta\tan\theta+b^{2}\sec^{2}\theta$. Subtracting, $x^{2}-y^{2}=a^{2}(\sec^{2}\theta-\tan^{2}\theta)-b^{2}(\sec^{2}\theta-\tan^{2}\theta)=(a^{2}-b^{2})\cdot 1=a^{2}-b^{2}$.

text: If $\operatorname{cosec}\theta-\sin\theta=a^{3}$ and $\sec\theta-\cos\theta=b^{3}$, prove that $a^{2}b^{2}(a^{2}+b^{2})=1$.
answer: $a^{3}=\frac{1}{\sin\theta}-\sin\theta=\frac{\cos^{2}\theta}{\sin\theta}$ and $b^{3}=\frac{1}{\cos\theta}-\cos\theta=\frac{\sin^{2}\theta}{\cos\theta}$. So $a=\frac{\cos^{2/3}\theta}{\sin^{1/3}\theta}$ and $b=\frac{\sin^{2/3}\theta}{\cos^{1/3}\theta}$, giving $a^{2}=\frac{\cos^{4/3}\theta}{\sin^{2/3}\theta}$, $b^{2}=\frac{\sin^{4/3}\theta}{\cos^{2/3}\theta}$. Then $a^{2}b^{2}=\sin^{2/3}\theta\cos^{2/3}\theta$ and $a^{2}+b^{2}=\frac{\cos^{2}\theta+\sin^{2}\theta}{\sin^{2/3}\theta\cos^{2/3}\theta}=\frac{1}{\sin^{2/3}\theta\cos^{2/3}\theta}$. Multiplying, $a^{2}b^{2}(a^{2}+b^{2})=1$.

text: If $x=1+2(\cos\theta+\sin\theta)$ and $y=2(\cos\theta-\sin\theta)-3$, prove that $(x-1)^{2}+(y+3)^{2}=8$.
answer: $x-1=2(\cos\theta+\sin\theta)$ and $y+3=2(\cos\theta-\sin\theta)$. So $(x-1)^{2}=4(\cos^{2}\theta+\sin^{2}\theta+2\sin\theta\cos\theta)=4(1+2\sin\theta\cos\theta)$ and $(y+3)^{2}=4(1-2\sin\theta\cos\theta)$. Adding, $(x-1)^{2}+(y+3)^{2}=4(1+1)=8$.

text: Prove that $\frac{\tan\theta}{1-\cot\theta}+\frac{\cot\theta}{1-\tan\theta}=1+\sec\theta\operatorname{cosec}\theta$.
answer: Write $\cot\theta=\frac{1}{\tan\theta}$ and let $t=\tan\theta$. First term $=\frac{t}{1-\frac{1}{t}}=\frac{t^{2}}{t-1}$. Second term $=\frac{\frac{1}{t}}{1-t}=-\frac{1}{t(t-1)}$. LHS $=\frac{t^{3}-1}{t(t-1)}=\frac{(t-1)(t^{2}+t+1)}{t(t-1)}=\frac{t^{2}+t+1}{t}=t+1+\frac{1}{t}=1+\tan\theta+\cot\theta$. Now $\tan\theta+\cot\theta=\frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}+\frac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}=\frac{\sin^{2}\theta+\cos^{2}\theta}{\sin\theta\cos\theta}=\frac{1}{\sin\theta\cos\theta}=\sec\theta\operatorname{cosec}\theta$. So LHS $=1+\sec\theta\operatorname{cosec}\theta=$ RHS.

text: If $\sec\theta-\tan\theta=x$, show that $\sec\theta=\frac{1}{2}\left(x+\frac{1}{x}\right)$ and $\tan\theta=\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{1}{x}-x\right)$. Hence express $\sin\theta$ in terms of $x$, and find $\sin\theta$ when $x=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$.
answer: Since $\sec^{2}\theta-\tan^{2}\theta=1$, $(\sec\theta-\tan\theta)(\sec\theta+\tan\theta)=1$, so $\sec\theta+\tan\theta=\frac{1}{x}$. Adding the two equations: $2\sec\theta=x+\frac{1}{x}$, so $\sec\theta=\frac{1}{2}\left(x+\frac{1}{x}\right)$. Subtracting: $2\tan\theta=\frac{1}{x}-x$, so $\tan\theta=\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{1}{x}-x\right)$. Then $\sin\theta=\frac{\tan\theta}{\sec\theta}=\frac{\frac{1}{x}-x}{\frac{1}{x}+x}=\frac{1-x^{2}}{1+x^{2}}$. For $x=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$: $x^{2}=\frac{1}{3}$, so $\sin\theta=\frac{1-\frac{1}{3}}{1+\frac{1}{3}}=\frac{2/3}{4/3}=\frac{1}{2}$. (Check: $\theta=30^\circ$ gives $\sec 30^\circ-\tan 30^\circ=\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$.)

answer: Correct option: A) $25\text{ m}$. $\tan 45^\circ=\frac{h}{25}$, so $h=25\times 1=25\text{ m}$.

answer: Correct option: B) $15\text{ m}$. $\tan 30^\circ=\frac{h}{15\sqrt{3}}$, so $h=15\sqrt{3}\times\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}=15\text{ m}$.

text: A building $20\sqrt{3}\text{ m}$ tall stands on level ground when the Sun's altitude is $60^\circ$. The length of its shadow is
answer: Correct option: A) $20\text{ m}$. $\tan 60^\circ=\frac{20\sqrt{3}}{s}$, so $s=\frac{20\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{3}}=20\text{ m}$.

answer: Correct option: B) $45^\circ$. The top is $21.6-1.6=20\text{ m}$ above eye level, so $\tan\theta=\frac{20}{20}=1$ and $\theta=45^\circ$.

answer: Correct option: D) $12\sqrt{3}\text{ m}$. Shadow at $30^\circ$: $\frac{18}{\tan 30^\circ}=18\sqrt{3}$; at $60^\circ$: $\frac{18}{\sqrt{3}}=6\sqrt{3}$. Decrease $=18\sqrt{3}-6\sqrt{3}=12\sqrt{3}\text{ m}$.

answer: Correct option: C) A is true but R is false. By Pythagoras, length $=\sqrt{7^{2}+24^{2}}=\sqrt{625}=25\text{ m}$, so A is true. The angle $\theta$ with the ground has $\tan\theta=\frac{24}{7}$, which is not $\sqrt{3}$, so R is false.

text: At a certain time of day, the shadow of a vertical pole on level ground is $\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$ times the height of the pole. Find the angle of elevation of the Sun at that time.
answer: Let the height be $h$; then the shadow is $\frac{h}{\sqrt{3}}$. If $\theta$ is the Sun's elevation, $\tan\theta=\frac{h}{h/\sqrt{3}}=\sqrt{3}$. Hence $\theta=60^\circ$.

text: A flagstaff $15\text{ m}$ high stands on level ground. At a certain moment, the tangent of the Sun's angle of elevation is $\frac{5}{4}$. Find the length of the shadow of the flagstaff.
answer: Let the shadow be $s$ m. $\tan\theta=\frac{15}{s}=\frac{5}{4}$, so $s=\frac{15\times 4}{5}=12$. The shadow is $12\text{ m}$ long.

text: An observer on the upper deck of a boat, $12\text{ m}$ above sea level, sees the top of a vertical cliff at an angle of elevation of $60^\circ$ and the foot of the cliff (at sea level) at an angle of depression of $30^\circ$. Find the height of the cliff and the horizontal distance of the boat from the cliff.
answer: Let the observer be at $E$, the foot of the cliff $F$ and its top $T$; let the horizontal distance be $d$. Draw the horizontal $EM$ from the eye to the cliff, so $MF=12\text{ m}$. Foot: $\tan 30^\circ=\frac{12}{d}$, so $d=12\sqrt{3}\text{ m}\approx 20.78\text{ m}$. Top: $\tan 60^\circ=\frac{TM}{d}$, so $TM=12\sqrt{3}\times\sqrt{3}=36\text{ m}$. Height of the cliff $=TM+MF=36+12=48\text{ m}$. The boat is $12\sqrt{3}\approx 20.78\text{ m}$ from the cliff (taking $\sqrt{3}=1.732$).

text: Two aeroplanes are flying one vertically above the other. The higher one is at a height of $3000\text{ m}$. From a point on the ground, the angles of elevation of the two aeroplanes are $60^\circ$ and $45^\circ$. Find the vertical distance between the aeroplanes. (Use $\sqrt{3}=1.732$.)
answer: Let $G$ be the ground point and $F$ the point directly below the aeroplanes, $GF=d$. Higher plane: $\tan 60^\circ=\frac{3000}{d}$, so $d=\frac{3000}{\sqrt{3}}=1000\sqrt{3}\text{ m}$. Lower plane at height $h$: $\tan 45^\circ=\frac{h}{d}$, so $h=d=1000\sqrt{3}\approx 1732\text{ m}$. Vertical gap $=3000-1000\sqrt{3}=1000(3-\sqrt{3})\approx 1000\times 1.268=1268\text{ m}$.

text: From the top of a lighthouse, the angles of depression of two ships, one exactly behind the other on the same side of the lighthouse, are $60^\circ$ and $30^\circ$. If the ships are $200\text{ m}$ apart, find the height of the lighthouse and the distance of the nearer ship from its foot. (Use $\sqrt{3}=1.732$.)
answer: Let the height be $h$, the nearer ship $A$ (depression $60^\circ$) at distance $x$ and the farther ship $B$ (depression $30^\circ$) at distance $x+200$. In the triangle with $A$: $\tan 60^\circ=\frac{h}{x}$, so $x=\frac{h}{\sqrt{3}}$. In the triangle with $B$: $\tan 30^\circ=\frac{h}{x+200}$, so $x+200=h\sqrt{3}$. Subtracting: $h\sqrt{3}-\frac{h}{\sqrt{3}}=200$, i.e. $\frac{2h}{\sqrt{3}}=200$, so $h=100\sqrt{3}\approx 173.2\text{ m}$. Nearer ship: $x=\frac{100\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{3}}=100\text{ m}$ from the foot.

text: A river is $100\text{ m}$ wide. From a point $P$ on a bridge directly above the river, the angles of depression of the two banks, on opposite sides of $P$, are $30^\circ$ and $60^\circ$. Find the height of $P$ above the water and the distance of each bank from the point on the water directly below $P$. (Use $\sqrt{3}=1.732$.)
answer: Let $M$ be the point on the water directly below $P$, $PM=h$, and let the banks be $A$ (depression $30^\circ$) and $B$ (depression $60^\circ$). $\tan 30^\circ=\frac{h}{AM}$, so $AM=h\sqrt{3}$. $\tan 60^\circ=\frac{h}{BM}$, so $BM=\frac{h}{\sqrt{3}}$. $AM+BM=100$: $h\sqrt{3}+\frac{h}{\sqrt{3}}=100$, so $\frac{4h}{\sqrt{3}}=100$ and $h=25\sqrt{3}\approx 43.3\text{ m}$. Then $AM=25\sqrt{3}\times\sqrt{3}=75\text{ m}$ and $BM=25\text{ m}$.

Find the height of the building, the distance between the building and the tower, and the straight-line distance from the top of the building to the top of the tower. (Use $\sqrt{3}=1.732$.)
answer: Let the building have height $h$ and let the distance between them be $d$. The horizontal from the top of the building meets the tower at a point $h$ above the ground. Depression of the foot: $\tan 60^\circ=\frac{h}{d}$, so $h=d\sqrt{3}$. Elevation of the top: $\tan 30^\circ=\frac{60-h}{d}$, so $60-h=\frac{d}{\sqrt{3}}$. Adding: $60=d\sqrt{3}+\frac{d}{\sqrt{3}}=\frac{4d}{\sqrt{3}}$, so $d=15\sqrt{3}\approx 25.98\text{ m}$ and $h=15\sqrt{3}\times\sqrt{3}=45\text{ m}$. text: From the top of a $60\text{ m}$ high tower, a man sees a cyclist riding straight towards the foot of the tower at an angle of depression of $30^\circ$. Ten seconds later the angle of depression is $45^\circ$. Assuming the cyclist rides at a constant speed, find (i) the distance covered in those $10$ seconds, (ii) the cyclist's speed in $\text{km/h}$, and (iii) how many more seconds the cyclist takes to reach the foot of the tower. (Use $\sqrt{3}=1.732$.)
answer: First position $A$: $\tan 30^\circ=\frac{60}{FA}$, so $FA=60\sqrt{3}\text{ m}$, where $F$ is the foot. Second position $B$: $\tan 45^\circ=\frac{60}{FB}$, so $FB=60\text{ m}$. (i) $AB=60\sqrt{3}-60=60(\sqrt{3}-1)=60\times 0.732=43.92\text{ m}$. (ii) Speed $=\frac{43.92}{10}=4.392\text{ m/s}=4.392\times\frac{18}{5}\approx 15.81\text{ km/h}$. (iii) Time for the remaining $60\text{ m}$ $=\frac{60}{6(\sqrt{3}-1)}=\frac{10}{\sqrt{3}-1}=5(\sqrt{3}+1)\approx 13.66$ seconds.

text: A drone flies in a straight horizontal line at a constant height of $40\sqrt{3}\text{ m}$ above level ground. An observer on the ground sees it in front of her at an angle of elevation of $60^\circ$. Eight seconds later, having passed over her head, the drone is seen behind her at an angle of elevation of $30^\circ$. Find the speed of the drone in $\text{m/s}$ and in $\text{km/h}$.
answer: Let $O$ be the observer, and $M$, $N$ the points on the ground directly below the two positions of the drone; they are on opposite sides of $O$. First position: $\tan 60^\circ=\frac{40\sqrt{3}}{OM}$, so $OM=40\text{ m}$. Second position: $\tan 30^\circ=\frac{40\sqrt{3}}{ON}$, so $ON=40\sqrt{3}\times\sqrt{3}=120\text{ m}$. Distance flown $=OM+ON=160\text{ m}$ in $8$ s. Speed $=\frac{160}{8}=20\text{ m/s}=20\times\frac{18}{5}=72\text{ km/h}$.

text: Two students $A$ and $B$ stand on level ground in a straight line with the point directly below a hovering drone, on the same side of it, with $B$ $40\text{ m}$ farther away than $A$. The angles of elevation of the drone from $A$ and $B$ are $45^\circ$ and $30^\circ$. Find (i) the height of the drone, (ii) its line-of-sight distance from $A$, and (iii) the horizontal distance of $B$ from the point below the drone. (Use $\sqrt{3}=1.732$, $\sqrt{2}=1.414$.)
answer: Let the drone be at height $h$ above the point $F$, and $FA=x$, so $FB=x+40$. From $A$: $\tan 45^\circ=\frac{h}{x}$, so $x=h$. From $B$: $\tan 30^\circ=\frac{h}{x+40}$, so $h\sqrt{3}=h+40$. answer: Let the distance between the feet be $d$ and the taller height $H$. From the foot of the taller tower: $\tan 30^\circ=\frac{15}{d}$, so $d=15\sqrt{3}\text{ m}\approx 25.98\text{ m}$. From the foot of the shorter tower: $\tan 60^\circ=\frac{H}{d}$, so $H=15\sqrt{3}\times\sqrt{3}=45\text{ m}$. The tops differ in height by $45-15=30\text{ m}$ and are $d$ apart horizontally, so wire $=\sqrt{(15\sqrt{3})^{2}+30^{2}}=\sqrt{675+900}=\sqrt{1575}=15\sqrt{7}\approx 39.69\text{ m}$.

text: A kite is flying $60\text{ m}$ above level ground. A girl standing at point $A$ on the ground holds a taut string to the kite, making an angle of $60^\circ$ with the ground. On the other side of the kite stands a building, whose foot is $60\sqrt{3}\text{ m}$ from $A$ along the ground. A boy on the roof of the building sees the kite at an angle of elevation of $30^\circ$. The kite lies between $A$ and the building. Find (i) the length of the girl's string, (ii) the height of the building, and (iii) the distance of the kite from the boy. (Use $\sqrt{3}=1.732$.)
answer: Let $K$ be the kite and $M$ the point on the ground below it. (i) $\sin 60^\circ=\frac{60}{AK}$, so $AK=\frac{60\times 2}{\sqrt{3}}=40\sqrt{3}\approx 69.28\text{ m}$. Also $AM=\frac{60}{\tan 60^\circ}=20\sqrt{3}\text{ m}$, so the horizontal distance from $M$ to the building is $60\sqrt{3}-20\sqrt{3}=40\sqrt{3}\text{ m}$. (ii) From the boy: height of the kite above the roof $=40\sqrt{3}\tan 30^\circ=40\text{ m}$. So the building is $60-40=20\text{ m}$ high. (iii) Distance from the boy $=\frac{40}{\sin 30^\circ}=80\text{ m}$.

text: The shadow of a vertical tower on level ground is $20\text{ m}$ longer when the Sun's altitude is $30^\circ$ than when it is $45^\circ$. Find the height of the tower and the length of its shadow when the altitude is $45^\circ$. (Use $\sqrt{3}=1.732$.)
answer: Let the height be $h$. At $45^\circ$ the shadow is $\frac{h}{\tan 45^\circ}=h$. At $30^\circ$ the shadow is $\frac{h}{\tan 30^\circ}=h\sqrt{3}$. Given $h\sqrt{3}-h=20$, so $h=\frac{20}{\sqrt{3}-1}=\frac{20(\sqrt{3}+1)}{2}=10(\sqrt{3}+1)\approx 27.32\text{ m}$. The shadow at $45^\circ$ equals the height, $\approx 27.32\text{ m}$.

text: A spherical balloon of radius $r$ subtends an angle of $60^\circ$ at the eye of an observer, and the angle of elevation of its centre from the eye is $60^\circ$. Prove that the height of the centre of the balloon above the eye is $\sqrt{3}\,r$, and find the horizontal distance of the centre from the observer in terms of $r$.
answer: Let $E$ be the eye and $C$ the centre. The two lines of sight from $E$ that just graze the balloon are tangents, touching it at $P$ and $Q$, with $\angle PEQ=60^\circ$. The line $EC$ bisects $\angle PEQ$, so $\angle PEC=30^\circ$, and the radius $CP\perp EP$ (radius is perpendicular to the tangent at the point of contact). In right $\triangle EPC$: $\sin 30^\circ=\frac{CP}{EC}=\frac{r}{EC}$, so $EC=2r$. Let $M$ be the point at eye level vertically below $C$. In right $\triangle EMC$ with $\angle CEM=60^\circ$: $CM=EC\sin 60^\circ=2r\times\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}=\sqrt{3}\,r$. Hence proved. Horizontal distance $EM=EC\cos 60^\circ=2r\times\frac{1}{2}=r$.

text: A ladder leans against a vertical wall and makes an angle of $60^\circ$ with the level ground. Its foot is then pulled $4\text{ m}$ further away from the wall, and the ladder now makes an angle of $30^\circ$ with the ground, its top still resting on the wall. Find the length of the ladder, how far its top slides down the wall, and the height it now reaches. (Use $\sqrt{3}=1.732$.)
answer: Let the ladder have length $l$. Distance of the foot from the wall: first $l\cos 60^\circ=\frac{l}{2}$, then $l\cos 30^\circ=\frac{\sqrt{3}\,l}{2}$. $\frac{\sqrt{3}\,l}{2}-\frac{l}{2}=4$, so $l=\frac{8}{\sqrt{3}-1}=4(\sqrt{3}+1)\approx 10.93\text{ m}$. Height reached: first $l\sin 60^\circ=\frac{\sqrt{3}\,l}{2}$, then $l\sin 30^\circ=\frac{l}{2}$. Slide $=\frac{\sqrt{3}\,l}{2}-\frac{l}{2}=\frac{(\sqrt{3}-1)l}{2}=\frac{(\sqrt{3}-1)\times 4(\sqrt{3}+1)}{2}=\frac{4\times 2}{2}=4\text{ m}$. New height $=\frac{l}{2}=2(\sqrt{3}+1)\approx 5.46\text{ m}$.

text: The top $T$ of a pavilion standing in a calm lake is $24\text{ m}$ above the water surface. A tourist on a lakeside platform at $P$, some height above the water, sees $T$ at an angle of elevation of $30^\circ$ and the reflection $T'$ of the top in the water at an angle of depression of $60^\circ$. $A$ is the point on the water surface directly below $P$, and $B$ is the point on the surface directly below $T$.
answer: (i) $BT'=24\text{ m}$; (ii) $\tan 30^\circ=\frac{24-h}{x}$, $\tan 60^\circ=\frac{24+h}{x}$; (iii) $h=12\text{ m}$, $x=12\sqrt{3}\approx 20.78\text{ m}$.

parts.label: (i)
parts.text: How far below the water surface does the reflection $T'$ appear to be?
parts.answer: A calm water surface acts as a plane mirror, so the image is as far below the surface as the object is above it: $BT'=BT=24\text{ m}$.

parts.label: (ii)
parts.text: Taking the height of $P$ above the water as $h$ m and the horizontal distance $AB$ as $x$ m, write two equations linking $h$ and $x$.
parts.answer: $T$ is $24-h$ above the level of $P$ and $T'$ is $24+h$ below it, so $\tan 30^\circ=\frac{24-h}{x}$ and $\tan 60^\circ=\frac{24+h}{x}$.

parts.label: (iii)
parts.text: Find the height of $P$ above the water and the horizontal distance of the pavilion from the platform.
parts.answer: Dividing the equations: $\frac{24+h}{24-h}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{1/\sqrt{3}}=3$, so $24+h=72-3h$ and $h=12\text{ m}$. Then $x=\sqrt{3}(24-h)=12\sqrt{3}\approx 20.78\text{ m}$ (using $\sqrt{3}=1.732$).
